1.pericope_label: Against false report, following a multitude, and partiality in judgment

schools.summary: Calvin allows both renderings but decides for 'receive' because the following clause forbids putting the hand with the wicked, and argues that a lie collapses of its own emptiness unless others take it up, so that raising and keeping up a calumny differ little; Gill makes the same point from the side of those ready to repeat what they hear.

Henry describes the Jewish bench where the junior voted first to escape his seniors' authority, refuses to confine the law to the courts since reputation lies at the mercy of any company without redress, and holds that foolish pity for a poor man's poverty is as much a perversion of judgment as fear of the great.

Clarke reports a third rendering, 'publish', and declines to choose between the three since inventor and receiver are almost equally criminal, turns the multitude clause into an argument for singularity while noting the word may mean the great rather than the many, and answers the third command with fiat justitia ruat coelum.

Keil and Delitzsch render the second command as a ban on testimony that sides with the majority to pervert justice, and use the parallel in Leviticus to overthrow Knobel's conjectural emendation of 'poor' to 'great'; Ellicott cites the Septuagint and Vulgate for 'receive', extends the ninth commandment from principals to accessories, and denies that Scripture anywhere sanctions the voice of the people as the voice of God.

debates: Whether the command forbids raising a false report, receiving one, or publishing it

4.pericope_label: Kindness to an enemy, and justice for the poor, the innocent and the stranger

schools.summary: Calvin makes negligence a species of theft, finds the command about an enemy's beast the strongest possible statement of how far from vengeance God would have his people stand, reads the obscure verse as putting enemies to work side by side and so giving them occasion for reconciliation, anticipates the objection that judges rarely favour the poor by pointing to ambition generous at another's expense, and holds that gifts infect a sound mind before they soil the hand; Gill dwells on the phrase 'thy poor'.

Clarke reads the law about the straying ox as the seed of the Sermon on the Mount, cites Magna Charta against the sale of justice, and presses the appeal to Israel's own memory of being strangers; Wesley reads the threat attached to the false matter as God condemning whoever unjustly condemns another.

Ellicott sets the law against the limits of classical ethics in Cicero, prefers Geddes' one-letter emendation in the disputed verse, reports Josephus on the death penalty for a bribed judge and traces corrupt justice to the captivity, and reads the repeated law on strangers as evidence of a standing national fault; Keil and Delitzsch paraphrase the disputed verse to the same practical sense and name the offence judicial murder.

debates: What the disputed verb in the verse about the fallen ass means, and whether the false-witness law belongs under the sixth commandment
outliers: Ellicott adopts Geddes' conjectural emendation of the text rather than construing the received reading

10.pericope_label: The sabbatical year, the weekly sabbath, and no mention of other gods

schools.summary: Gill makes the seventh-year rest a declaration that God owned the land and Israel only held it; Calvin treats the sabbath's benefit to household and cattle as incidental to its institution but a real blessing, and turns the clause on masters who had themselves been slaves, while tying the ban on naming other gods to the third commandment, since swearing by a god makes it the judge of souls.

Henry gives three purposes for the year of rest, guards the weekly sabbath against being absorbed into it, and reads the opening caution as covering the whole chapter, that carelessness can ruin a man where only circumspection can save him.

Clarke reports Calmet's five reasons for the sabbatical year, works out the arithmetic of the threefold harvest promised in Leviticus, observes that the ordinance's observance is nowhere recorded and infers the captivity gave the land the sabbaths unbelief had denied it, presses the sabbath's mercy toward worked animals, and glosses 'refreshed' as re-souled.

Keil and Delitzsch place the year of rest and the sabbath among mutual obligations rather than among the feasts, since the care of the poor stands foremost in both; Ellicott shows how far the levelling of the seventh year went, reads the sabbath and sabbatical year as one system culminating in the jubilee, and qualifies the ban on naming other gods by noting that Moses himself names several.

debates: Whether the ban on mentioning other gods forbids swearing by them or naming them at all
outliers: Clarke infers from the silence of the historical books that the sabbatical year was largely never kept

14.pericope_label: The three annual feasts, and the rules that govern them

schools.summary: Calvin asks where the feast of trumpets and the day of atonement have gone if only three appearances are commanded, answers that the seventh month's holy days fell within one journey, derives from the number a rule that God requires no service which does not come from a cheerful heart, and refuses the dietary reading of the kid entirely, assigning the precept to the sacrifices; Gill preserves the Mishnaic list of those exempt from appearing.

Clarke identifies the three feasts and their memorials, adds Calmet on why festivals were appointed and a catalogue of the lesser ones, reports Cudworth's Karaite manuscript on the magical use of a kid boiled in its dam's milk, and concludes that the precept forbids whatever blunts the moral feelings; Wesley explains why the feasts avoid winter and harvest and infers that servants were exempt since none might appear empty.

Keil and Delitzsch restrict the obligation to numbered males without excluding women and boys, and read the leaven rule of the paschal lamb; Ellicott details the later observance of Pentecost and ingathering, prefers 'the fat of my feast', and refutes the magical explanation of the kid from Deuteronomy in favour of Bochart's account of its cruelty.

debates: Why the kid was not to be seethed in its mother's milk, and whether the precept concerns diet or sacrifice
outliers: Ellicott calls the magical-rite explanation that Clarke and Wesley report a fanciful exegesis; Calvin rejects the dietary reading that all the others assume

20.pericope_label: The Angel sent before Israel, and the promises attached to obedience

schools.summary: Calvin argues at length that the Angel cannot be Joshua, rests the case on Paul's warning not to tempt Christ, makes the indwelling Name the decisive proof since it grants knowledge of hearts and power of judgment, catches the wordplay by which the Angel's keeping answers Israel's keeping of itself, distinguishes the permanent condemnation of superstition from the temporary order to demolish, and follows Augustine in denying private men any commission to destroy idols; Gill collects the rabbinic identifications from Michael to Metatron.

Henry sets the created-angel and Son-of-God readings side by side without deciding, holds that Christ saves only those who obey him, reads the promise against Israel's enemies as a league offensive and defensive after the pattern of Abraham's, and counts the four blessings of food, health, increase and length of days.

Clarke rules out Moses and Joshua and quotes Philo on the only-begotten Son as viceroy over the flock, valuing the testimony because its author was no Christian, notes that six nations stand here where other texts give seven, and says the meanest fare suffices when God's blessing is in it.

Keil and Delitzsch take the Name in the Angel to mean that Jehovah revealed himself in him; Ellicott reports Kalisch's identification with Moses only to reject it, argues that God is never said to set his Name in a man, distinguishes cutting nations down from exterminating them, and holds that the Canaanites were expelled for profligacy rather than idolatry.

debates: Whether the Angel sent before Israel is a created being, Moses or Joshua, or the pre-incarnate Son
outliers: Calvin infers from this passage that churches once polluted by idols may lawfully be retained and put to better use

27.pericope_label: The fear and the hornets, the gradual conquest, and no covenant with the nations

schools.summary: Calvin makes the fear an inward work of God who holds courage and cowardice alike in his hand, cites Rahab as a witness who went only halfway, takes the hornets for a proof that God arms his least creatures, finds mercy in the slowness of the conquest and fault in Israel's slackness, and follows the promised bounds through David to Christ, adding that the Gentiles filled a place the Jews left empty; Gill reports the rival readings of the hornets and draws a parallel with corruption left in the converted.

Clarke argues the hornets literal from the creature's size and ferocity and from his own failure to hold one in forceps, holds that the promised bounds were reached only under Solomon because men are slow to believe, grounds the ban on covenants in Israel's office of keeping true religion until the Messiah, and closes by urging the reader to love his enemy; Wesley states briefly that they who fear will soon flee.

Keil and Delitzsch know the precedents for insect plagues and still refuse a literal reading, since Joshua records no such extermination; Ellicott proposes that the hornets are the Egyptians whose armies broke the Hittites, notes the Egyptian hieroglyph of a bee for king, confirms the danger of an emptied land from the lions that followed Assyria's deportation of Samaria, and explains the ban on covenants from treaties that acknowledged each other's gods.

debates: Whether the hornets are literal insects, a wasting disease, the terror already promised, or the armies of Egypt
